clues.title: Road line: Long outer lines
text: If you see long dashed outer lines, you'll know it's Norway. You can find similar dashed lines with the same climate in Sweden, but they will be half the length, and Finland uses full outer lines.
(N)orway for normal, (S)weden for short, and (F)inland for full.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Long yellow-orange middle lines
text: Many larger roads in Norway have solid outer lines and yellow middle lines. The yellow lines have a distinct tinge of orange, making them easily recognizable.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Language - Sámi Signs
text: Bilingual signs with **Sámi** can be found in several northern areas in Norway. While the Sámi languages are very different from Norwegian, the best way to recognize them are the letters Á, Đ and the use of several vowels in a row, something which is uncommon in Norwegian. Note that not all signs in these areas will be bilingual.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Vegetation: Vegetation - Bracken
text: This species of fern ( Pteridium aquilinum , also known as **bracken**) which typically has a fairly tall stem and many wide leafs branching out, is mostly found in the south of Norway. Beware that other species of ferns can be found further north.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Vegetation: Vegetation - Spruce
text: **Spruces** are mainly found in the southern half of the country, particularly in the southeast and around Trondheim.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Vegetation: Vegetation - Pine
text: **Pines** are most common in coastal and far inland areas in the southern half of the country.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Vegetation: Vegetation - Oaks
text: **Oaks** are mainly found in the far south of Norway.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Vegetation: Vegetation - Maple
text: **Maples** are mainly found in the south, particularly by the farmlands around Oslo.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Vegetation: Vegetation - Bright Moss
text: **Brightly colored moss** is common to find in the area between **Lillehammer** and **Oppdal**

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Oslo Farmlands
text: The largest concentration of farmland is found in the southeast, in the general vicinity of Oslo. The area is **much flatter** than most of the country, and it is common to get a rolling landscape with smooth, round forested hills in the distance. The area southeast of Oslo is particularly flat.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Trondheim Farmlands
text: The farmlands surrounding Trondheim are generally **very hilly**, and the hills are typically both steeper and more uneven than in the southeast.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Stavanger Farmlands
text: The farmland south of Stavanger is flatter than most of the country. The fields look **vast** and open, and it is very common to see **rock walls** made of large, round rocks. Furthermore, rather than crops, most fields will only contain grass.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Deep Fjords
text: While fjords can be found along most of the Norwegian coast, **deep fjords** surrounded by **tall mountains** are most common between **Bergen** and **Trondheim**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Lofoten Mountains
text: Distinct, **sharp, rocky** mountains with few trees can be seen on the Lofoten Archipelago.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Northeastern Landscape
text: The northeast of Norway can typically be recognized by a somewhat **rolling landscape**, rather than tall mountains, and vegetation mainly consisting of very **small birches** combined with patched grass.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Highlands
text: Barren highlands, with **no trees or bushes**, and often with rocky mountains along the road, are mostly found in the southwest.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Exposed Rock
text: **Exposed rock**, often spotted with small coastal pines and bushes, is mainly found on the south coast.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Northern Coastal Grasslands
text: **Coastal grasslands** with little to no other vegetation and only somewhat low, distant mountains can be found by coastal roads in the far north.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - White House Village
text: While completely **white wooden houses** can be found in the entire country, they're especially common on the southern coast, where you'll commonly see entire villages made up of them.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Infrastructure - Black Snow Poles
text: **Black plastic snowpoles** are more regional and will mostly be found in Trøndelag, Møre og Romsdal and Vestland, but can also be found in Nordland and more rarely in Innlandet, Buskerud, Rogaland and Telemark

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Infrastructure - Wide Black ID
text: Small, **wide black pole plates**, with a single line of letters and digits, can be found in southeastern Norway.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Guardrail: Infrastructure - Rusty Guardrail
text: **Rusty guardrails** are almost exclusively found in coastal regions, and particularly on the southern half of the west coast.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Russian Border Road
text: Along the Russian border you can see this noticeably humid and green-looking road, with very overcast and occasionally foggy coverage. The trees are somewhat low and mainly consist of thin birches and pines.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Infrastructure - Oslo Pole Plate
text: Fairly large **black or red pole plates** can be found in Oslo.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Infrastructure - Two Red Stripes
text: **Two red stripes** going around lamp posts are commonly found in Stavanger.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Infrastructure - Bergen Hydrant
text: You can find this specific design of **green fire hydrants** in Bergen.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Language: Language - Russian language
text: **Russian** can sometimes be seen alongside Norwegian on signs near the Russian border. It is mostly found on roads E6 and E105 near Kirkenes.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture - Røros Architecture
text: The old mining town of Røros can be recognised by the **densely built** traditional wooden architecture.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Pole: Infrastructure - Bamboo Snow Pole
text: **Bamboo** snowpoles are regional and can mostly be found in Innlandet, Akershus, Østfold, Buskerud and Vestfold but can also be found rarely in Trøndelag, Vestland, Agder, Telemark and Rogaland.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Infrastructure - Small Blue Snowpole
text: **Small blue snowpoles** can be found around Elverum.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Infrastructure - Senja Snowpoles
text: **Green plastic snowpoles** are found mostly around the island of Senja in Troms since the company selling these is also located there. The company also sells other colors less frequently. These can also less commonly be found all over Troms and Finnmark.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Infrastructure - Big Wooden Snowpole
text: **Big wooden sticks** are found on roads that are covered with snow almost the entire year. So far, they've been spotted on the road that runs north of Hardangervidda National Park, on the road west of Jotunheimen and southwest of Valdres Natur-og kulturpark.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Coverage: Coverage Meta - Thick Snow Road
text: This road between Aadneram and Nomeland in Agder features a **thick 1m high snow** along the **skinny road**. You will **not find trees** along this road.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - 82 (Andoya)
text: The 82 on the island of Andoya, which is part of the Lofoten archipelago, is **flat** apart from **one tabletop looking hill**. In generall, the hills on this road are quite unique and recognizable. You will find **short scrubs** along the road. Often, you will be able to see **water**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - E10, East of Narvik
text: This road is **very green** and usually features **big mountains with no trees**. Right on the Swedish border you will find parts without trees.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - E10 in Lofoten
text: This road features **huge mountains**. It is a **skinny road** that has **water to the east**. Lots of sections have **bridges** or **open tunnels**. You will frequently find **fireweed** on the sides of the road. The vegetation on this road has a **yellowish tone**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - E10 on the border of Troms and Nordland
text: This road **runs through a valley**. You can see a **big mountain range along the road**, with **no trees on the mountain**. Some sections are **very green**, and some section feature **fireweed**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Lysevegen
text: Lysevegen is a **very windy and skinny road** with 28 180° turns down the mountain. Notably, there are **big power lines** visible. You can see **huge mountains** in the distance. The coverage is **very cloudy**.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - End of the World Road
text: This famous road can be identified by the **lack of trees** and the **small white rocks**. The visibility in the coverage is somewhat low. Some sections are very flat, while others can have small hills and lakes.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Atlanterhavsveien
text: This road uses **dark rocks** as bridges. You will see **water on both sides of the road**. The coverage features **dark clouds**.
The road includes the famous Storseisundet bridge.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Røst Island
text: This island has only **Gen 2** coverage. You will see **lots of boats everywhere**. The landscape is **flat** and **islandish** (duh).

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Landscape: Landscape - Trollstigen
text: Trollstigen leads down a **huge mountain**, and is surrounded by such. The road is **very steep and windy**. The rock is **very dark** and has **green moss** on it. Some sections are cut into the rock, with waterfalls appearing.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Coverage: Coverage Meta - Snow Road
text: The road between Atna and Ringebu in Innlandet is **completely covered in snow**. You will find a **winter wonderland with green rocks**

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Plate: Green Plates
text: In Norway, **commercial** plates are **green**. These can often be seen on **vans** or **big trucks**(not semi-trucks).
NOTE: Within Europe, green licence plates are most commonly seen in Norway, but can also be found on electric vehicles in several other countries.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Stop sign: Norway bus stop sign
text: Norwegian bus stops usually have this small, blue sign with a white bus.
NOTE: Sweden has a lot of different bus stops, none of which look like this.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Road line: Roadlines

clues.title: Road line: Long Dashed Roadlines
text: Smaller Norwegian roads typically have long dashed white outer lines, while larger roads have solid outer lines and yellow middle lines.
The yellow lines have a distinct tinge of orange.
Sweden only has white road lines, and the dashes on outer lines are shorter than in Norway.
Finnish outer road lines are always solid, and middle lines can be yellow or white.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.title: Architecture: Architecture
text: Many houses are painted red, which is also typical for Sweden and Finland.
Black painted houses are also quite common, more so than in Sweden or Finland.
Sweden and Finland generally have more red and yellow houses, while Norway generally has more white houses.

clues.title: Sign: Centered Top Sign Posts
text: Street signs will generally be centred on top of sign posts.

clues.title: Landscape: Vast Farmland
text: Large farmlands are mainly found in three areas, the southeast, the area surrounding Trondheim, and south of Stavanger.
The following clues will explain how to differentiate between the three.

The largest concentration of farmland is found in the southeast, in the general vicinity of Oslo. The area is much flatter than most of the country, and it is common to get a rolling landscape with smooth, round forested hills in the distance. The area southeast of Oslo is particularly flat.
The farmlands surrounding Trondheim are generally very hilly, and the hills are typically both steeper and more uneven than in the southeast.

Similarly to the southeast, the farmland south of Stavanger is flatter than most of the country. However, the fields look more vast and open, and it is very common to see rock walls made of large, round rocks. Furthermore, rather than crops, most fields will only contain grass.

clues.title: Language: Norwegian
text: Norwegian is a North Germanic language closely related to Danish and Swedish. The Norwegian alphabet contains these special letters: **Æ, Ø**, and **Å**.
NOTE:
Danish also uses **Æ, Ø**, and **Å**.

Swedish only uses **Å**. In addition, Swedish uses **Ä** and **Ö**, not found in Norwegian. Norwegian uses more E’s than Swedish, while Swedish uses more A’s. Norwegian uses **kk** where Swedish uses **ck**.
Faroese uses **Æ and Ø** but not **Å**.
Icelandic only uses **Æ**.
The Norwegian word for road is **vei** or **veien** (or **veg/vegen**, depending on spelling). This is unlike Swedish which uses **väg** or **vägen** and Danish which uses **vej**.
The Norwegian word for street is **gate, gata** or rarely **gaten**. In Swedish it is **gatan** or, sometimes, **gata** aswell. Danish uses **gade**.
